BME 2081C: Electric Circuits / Ninetales Soldering and Testing Guide



                                    BME 2081C: Electric Circuits
                                Ninetales Soldering and Testing Guide


Name: ____________________________________________

Grade: out of 100 points and worth 1% of your final grade. However, you will need a successfully
soldered board in order to complete the other parts of this assignment which are worth a larger
percentage of your grade.

Objectives: Solder Ninetales so you can utilize it for your lab project.

NOTE: There is no partial credit for this assignment. Your circuit board either works or it doesn’t. If it
works, you get all the points. If it doesn’t work, you get 0 points.




                                      Figure 1. Image of Ninetales.




                                                                                                                    1

BME 2081C: Electric Circuits / Ninetales Soldering and Testing Guide



Part I: Please adhere to these safety guidelines
    1. Read and abide by the CEAS Solder Safety guidelines (Canvas: Home/Modules ->
         Soldering). In particular, please wear pants, closed-toed shoes, and a natural fiber long-
         sleeved shirt to the soldering session. Wear the safety glasses provided to you by your
         instructor for the duration of the soldering session, even if you’re not currently soldering.

    2. Only use the lead-free solder provided to you by your instructors.

    3. The soldering iron is hot. Please hold the iron by the black handle and not the silver tip.

    4. Do not leave your iron on for more than 10 minutes even if you’re in between soldering
       joints. If you leave the iron on for too long, you will oxidize the tip, rendering the tip useless.
       You can try to “tin” your tip by applying a small amount of solder to it and cleaning it with
       the brass sponge. However, if your tip is too corroded, it will need to be replaced.

    5. Use a fume extractor while you’re soldering to avoid the fumes from entering your
       respiratory system. The fume extractors are equipped with activated carbon filters which
       break down the organic molecules that cause respiratory irritation.

    6. If you use isopropyl alcohol to clean the flux off your board, wear gloves.


Part II: Setting up your soldering iron




   Figure 2. Picture of the soldering station control unit indicating the location of the ON/OFF switch.

    1. Turn your soldering iron on using the switch at the bottom, right side of the machine.

    2. Set your soldering iron to 660 degrees Fahrenheit. (The units on the machine are °F, not °C.)
           a. Press and hold the ENTER button until the hundreds digit starts flashing on the
              display. Use the UP button to change the hundreds digit (the numbers wrap around
              from 7 back to 0).


                                                                                                                    3

BME 2081C: Electric Circuits / Ninetales Soldering and Testing Guide



           b. Once the hundreds digit is set, press (don’t hold) the ENTER button again to switch
              to the tens digit. Then repeat step 3a. (The tens digit wraps around from 9 to 0.)

           c. Once the tens digit is set, press (don’t hold) the ENTER button to switch to the ones
              digit. Then repeat step 3b.

           d. Once the ones digit is set, press ENTER to finish.

   3. Allow your iron 2-3 minutes to warm up.

   4. You may increase the temperature of your soldering iron to 680 degrees Fahrenheit if your
      solder isn’t readily melting.


Part III: Helpful soldering tips
    1. Solder surface mount components before through-hole components.

   2. Solder lowest profile components before taller components.

   3. Solder passives (components that don’t need power, i.e., resistors, capacitors, inductors)
      before other components.

   4. You should CONSTANTLY be cleaning your soldering iron tip. Your instructors clean their
      irons every time they solder a single new connection. If you don’t have a clean tip (it’s not
      shiny), the solder won’t stick to the iron very well, and you’ll have quite a bit of difficulty
      getting anything done.

   5. Your soldering iron is not a writing utensil (pen or pencil). You want to place the iron so that
      you get good surface area contact between the iron and the components. So, hold your iron
      roughly sideways while soldering. Do not hold the iron like you’re using it as a pen or pencil.
      You won’t get good heat transfer and won’t be able to get anything done.

   6. Flux is your friend. Use it liberally. There shouldn’t be a pool of flux on your board, but the
      boards should be very damp.

Part IV: Gather Your Components

You’ve been provided with a 3D printed component box to store your components along with some
sharpies and labeling tape. Since you’ll solder Ninetales over the course of a few weeks, please start
by organizing your components into your component box. You will also be provided a larger project
box to store your components and your in-progress PCB over the course of the next few weeks. The
PCB will not fit inside the component box.

Part V: Soldering Ninetales

Steps
   1. Please read all the steps in their entirety before you start soldering.

   2. Obtain a Ninetales printed circuit board (PCB) from your instructors along with the
      components to solder to the board (Figure 3, Figure 4, and Table 2). The PCBs and other
      components may also be in a pick-up area designated by the instructor.

   3. Solder the components in the following order: resistors, capacitors, operational amplifiers,
      4-position headers (or 2, 2-position headers), 1-position headers, J9, J2, J3, LEDs, stackable
      headers. Consult the designator reference list on the final page of this document and the
      images in the proceeding pages.

   4. When you are soldering J1, J8, J4, J5, J6, J7, J10, J11, etc., insert the header pins into the
      designated vias. Tape the header pins down. Flip the board over, then solder the
      components to the board. It would be helpful to solder J1, J8, and J4 (4-position headers, or
      2, 2-position headers) at the same time and J5, J6, J7, J10, and J11 (1-position headers) at
      the same time.

   5. When soldering the 8-pin operational amplifiers, please consult Figure 8 and Figure 9 a few
      pages below.

   6. When soldering the LEDs, please consult Figure 10 a few pages below.

   7. When soldering the header pins, please consult Figure 11 a few pages below.

   8. A few reminders.
          a. Resistors: The black side of the resistor should face upwards. Also, the resistor is
              non-polar. It doesn’t matter how you rotate it (along its long axis).
          b. Capacitors: The capacitors are non-polar. It doesn’t matter which side you solder
              them along their long axis. The capacitor is also the same all the way around. It
              doesn’t matter how you rotate it around its center axis.

   9. Please have your instructors inspect your soldering job before you proceed.

   10. If instructors think your soldering job looks good, they will hand you three sets of sensor
       cables and ECG electrodes (Figure 6). The sensor cables will plug into the corresponding
       receptable on Ninetales based on which biosignal you are measuring. The locations for the
       electrodes and sensor cables are shown in Table 3 on the following page.

Steps
   1. When testing Ninetales, disconnect your computer from the wall outlet or anything that is
      connected to a wall outlet (like an external monitor).


      2. To test Ninetales, please find the example codes under the Home/Modules ->
         Ninetales on Canvas. You will need the following codes: EXAMPLE01_Blink.ino

         and EXAMPLE03_MultiSample.ino. If there are additional example codes on Canvas,
         you’ll use those at a later time (or they may just be for reference), but you don’t need them
         for this step.

      3. Please follow the instructions in the comments in each file. You should test
         EXAMPLE01_Blink.ino first and then EXAMPLE03_MultiSample.ino. and
         demonstrate each to your instructor. Your instructors will monitor you closely during this
         step, since the physiological signals are fairly nuanced, and we want to make sure they’re
         being acquired correctly.

      4. For the MultiSample test, we can essentially test the electrocardiogram (ECG) on all 3
         channels for convenience. The channels “overlap,” with which biosignal they are sensitive to
         (as explained in the MultiSample code). But be sure you read the instructions in each
         code as there is quite a bit of background information in each.

      5. Please see examples of what the physiological signals will look like in Figure 7.

      6. You may find that braiding the sensor cables helps to reduce noise.


Once the instructors say your board works…
   1. You are complete when the instructors inform you that your board is working as expected.
       Keep Ninetales, the sensor cables, and ECG electrodes. You’ll need them for your project.
       There’s nothing for you to submit on Canvas. Your instructors will mark your grade on Canvas
       themselves.

      2. Clean up your soldering station. Put everything you took out of the soldering kit, back inside
         the kit EXCEPT the physical iron (and the iron holder). We need to let the iron cool down
         before we put the hot iron back inside a plastic tote (for obvious reasons). Leave the kit on
         your desk, unplug the soldering station control unit, and place the unit back inside your
         kit.

Appendix C: Visual Guide for Soldering Operational Amplifiers




             (A)                                                 (B)




     (C)                            (D)                                 (E)




                      (F)                              (G)
Figure 8. Possible locations of the op amp’s pin 1 indicator. Images are showing the LM358; however, you
will be using the MCP6002 and AD8226. The guide still holds for the MCP6002 and AD8226 op amps, but
                     of course, the writing on the op amp will be different than Fig. 5B.

   1. When soldering the operational amplifiers (op amps), place flux on all the op amps pads on
      the PCB. Align your op amps on the pads with pin 1 placed in the top left corner (as
      indicated in Figure 8 and also detailed below). Apply flux on top of the op amp’s pins (in
      addition to the flux you added directly to the pads on the PCB earlier). Then solder the pin
      to the board.

           The pin 1 indicator for the op amps is indicated by either:

                    i. a circle in the top left corner, right next to pin 1 (or a circular indent or
                       “dimple”) (Figure 8A-C)

                    ii. a notch in the top center of the op amp. Pin 1 is to the left of the notch if you
                        position the notch to the top side of the op amp (Figure 8D).

                   iii. a line (or indent) on the left side of the op amp. Pin 1 is in the top left corner


                                                                                                                  13

BME 2081C: Electric Circuits / Ninetales Soldering and Testing Guide



                   if the line (or indent) is on the left side of the op amp (Figure 8E).

               iv. by a line at the top of the op amp. Pin 1 is to the left of the line (Figure 8F).

               v. if you have the part number oriented such that you can read it from right to
                  left, pin 1 is going to be to the bottom left of the part number (Figure 8G).

2. Then, add more flux to the top of the remaining 7 pins of the op amp (yes, in addition to the
   flux you added directly to the pads of the PCB earlier) and solder the remaining 7 pins. Yes,
   you must solder all 8 pins of the op amp for the op amp to function correctly. And, no,
   you’re not just adding one big blob of solder that’s connecting all the pins together. That’s
   called a “solder bridge” or a short.

       If you have any “solder bridges” (Figure 9) (connecting two pins together accidentally)
       between the pins of your op amp, please add more flux, then apply heat. That can often
       remove the bridges. If that doesn’t work, try using desoldering wick. Place the wick on
       top of the solder bridge. Then apply the soldering iron on top of the wick. Wait for 5-10
       seconds. It’s often helpful to have the soldering iron at slightly higher temperature
       (maybe an additional 50 oF) since the heat now must transfer from the iron to the wick,
       and then to the pin and pad.




    Figure 9. Notice the solder bridge between the two pins of the op amp. DON’T DO THIS.
                 Image courtesy of All About Circuits and SparkFun Electronics.
